title: Struggling Readers Who Speak African-American English Need Support—And Respect
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler reports on research by speech pathologist Julie Washington and cognitive scientist Mark Seidenberg on why many Black children who speak African American English face extra hurdles learning to read. The differences between AAE and General American English can obscure the correspondence between spoken and written language, for example when a child pronounces cold as cole. Wexler stresses that teachers should read slower responses as translation effort rather than lower ability, and should teach GAE without implying AAE is inferior, as the story of Dasani illustrates. She notes that bilingual-style curricula have helped, and that language variation tracks poverty and a continuum of density. She closes by tying the issue to weak phonics instruction and to curricula that do not build academic knowledge and vocabulary through read-alouds for all children.
points: Washington and Seidenberg argue that dialect-to-text translation is a real cognitive load that helps explain persistent reading gaps.
Slower responses from AAE speakers reflect translation effort, not lesser capability.
Instruction should teach General American English without framing AAE as incorrect or inferior.
A bilingual-style curriculum at one majority-Black school raised reading pass rates by 75%.
Ineffective phonics teaching and knowledge-poor curricula compound the difficulty for all children.
quotes: Merely charmed at first, Washington later realized what an extraordinary cognitive effort it took for the child to absorb the story in a version of English she didn’t speak and then translate it into her own version to retell it. It occurred to Washington that having to jump through those cognitive hoops could pose serious problems for many Black children—and help explain the persistent gap in reading test scores between them and their white peers.

Teachers need to understand that AAE-speakers may read or respond to questions more slowly, the authors say, not because they’re less capable but because they need more time to translate between dialects. And while children need to learn GAE in order to read, write, and communicate orally in certain settings, teachers should avoid making them feel that AAE is incorrect or inferior.

At the same time, programs designed to help speakers of other languages grasp English grammar can also help AAE-speakers. After one majority-Black elementary school that Washington studied implemented a “bilingual curriculum,” the number of students who passed state reading tests increased by 75%.

Dasani’s experience may have been particularly difficult because of the immersive nature of the school: students live in surrogate families with house parents who require the use of GAE around the clock. It may be easier for children to code-switch when they can slip back into the language variety they’re used to at home. But even in the typical school environment, teachers need to be able to teach GAE without conveying the idea that AAE is inferior.

Beyond that, it’s worth remembering that because of deficiencies in their training, teachers often use methods of reading instruction that don’t work even for many GAE-speakers. Because they don’t teach phonics effectively, those approaches are even less likely to work for speakers of other varieties of English.
